claims.claim: Some Nippur temple-linked rights were specified as recurring periods within a year, rather than undifferentiated full-time offices.
claims.date: Samsuiluna 11–12 in the directly dated core
claims.context: Martu/Kusu transactions; no secure household loci
claims.primary: G-I01–02: BE 6/2 36 and 39. G-I09 is lower-resolution corroboration.
claims.secondary: Poebel’s functional glosses are not required to establish the written annual periods.
claims.counter: Annual periods do not prove exact days worked, a universal rota, or the same calendar in all texts.
claims.limit: The particular rights described, not every Nippur institution.
claims.relevance: Separates a family-held entitlement from a presumed lifetime occupation.

claims.claim: The selected Nippur corpus attests both sale and exchange of temple-office rights.
claims.secondary: S04 abstract identifies the topic, but is not evidentiary support for the individual transactions.
claims.counter: No proof that all offices were freely alienable or that no eligibility/approval conditions existed.
claims.limit: Documented conveyances, not an unrestricted citywide market regime.
claims.relevance: Institutional connection could change through transactions as well as kinship.

claims.claim: Office-linked rights could form part of family patrimony alongside other assets, without all family property necessarily merging.
claims.context: Inherited Martu rights, paternal recovery, adoption and estate division
claims.primary: G-I01, G-I04, G-I08; G-I10 supplies catalogue-level corroboration.
claims.secondary: Archive-scale strategies are a further reconstruction, not directly stated.
claims.counter: A shared father does not prove co-residence; inheritance is not equivalent to inalienability.
claims.limit: Named property-holding cases; no prevalence estimate.
claims.relevance: Links institutional resources to durable family histories.

claims.claim: Two exchanges balance unequal office/land packages with silver, demonstrating negotiated equivalence in those transactions.
claims.primary: G-I02–03: BE 6/2 39 has 5 shekels; no. 37 has 2 shekels.
claims.counter: Mixed assets, damaged terms and differing temples prevent a standardized price comparison.
claims.limit: Two transaction-specific adjustments; not annual earnings or a price index.
claims.relevance: Shows connections between office rights, land and liquid resources.

claims.claim: Some Nippur reacquisitions explicitly characterize the recovered resource as belonging to the paternal house.
claims.date: BE 6/2 45 = Samsuiluna 14/12; no. 66 exact date not recovered
claims.context: Office recovery and a titled woman’s land recovery
claims.secondary: Poebel calls these redemptions; a compulsory family redemption rule is not established.
claims.counter: His Biblical analogy cannot supply a Nippur legal rule; causes of the earlier alienations are unknown.
claims.confidence: HIGH for the family-recovery language; MODERATE for legal mechanism
claims.limit: Two deeds and their stated family reference, not all lineage property.
claims.relevance: Continuity may include reacquisition after alienation.

claims.claim: A Nippur adoption deed protects specified office/property rights of the adoptee against claims by the named adoptive brother.
claims.primary: G-I08: BE 6/2 57, property and no-claim clauses.
claims.secondary: Later edition located but not read; identification of every earlier relationship remains provisional.
claims.counter: The deed does not establish that adoption transferred priestly qualification or actual cultic duty.
claims.limit: One explicit contractual arrangement; not a standard motive for all adoption.
claims.relevance: Created kinship and institutional patrimony could be negotiated together.

claims.claim: A woman bearing a Ninurta-related religious title is documented recovering paternal-house land from another similarly titled woman.
claims.primary: G-I07: title, patronymics, field recovery, silver consideration.
claims.secondary: Exact modern interpretation of SAL-ISḪIB is left open.
claims.counter: Religious affiliation does not make the field temple-owned or prove a female prebend sale.
claims.limit: Named titled women; no statement about all women’s access to every office.
claims.relevance: Women’s institutional affiliation and family property action can coexist.

claims.claim: One Ninlil-related family dispute records royal referral to Nippur’s council followed by a house/property settlement.
claims.primary: G-I05: BE 6/2 10, lines 1–36; S12 identifies P259799.
claims.secondary: Poebel’s wider theory of the council is not adopted.
claims.counter: A recorded royal referral is not evidence that every dispute followed this route or that this was a modern appellate hierarchy.
claims.limit: The route documented by this deed and its account of prior proceedings.
claims.relevance: Family-held institutional rights could involve multiple legal authorities.
